title: Impact of climate change on the spread of fascioliasis into the extreme south of South America
content: Fascioliasis, a highly pathogenic disease caused by Fasciola hepatica, has been spreading into the extreme south of South America. The disease, which affects humans and animals, is transmitted by freshwater snails and has a significant economic and sanitary impact. The increasing importance of human fascioliasis is due to its high pathogenicity and immunosuppressive capacity. The World Health Organization has listed fascioliasis as one of the Foodborne Trematodiases prioritized in the Neglected Tropical Diseases Roadmaps for 2020 and 2030. The current state of global emergence/re-emergence of fascioliasis appears to be related to the impact of climate and global change. In South America, fascioliasis has been identified as one of the diseases to be affected in more complex ways by climate and global changes. The study suggests that global warming may be the underlying cause allowing for the establishment of long-term transmission foci of fascioliasis in southernmost areas. The authors aim to analyze the evolution of local climate change factors of the last 65-year period to conclude whether their impact might have been the cause of the southward expansion of the fascioliasis endemic area into most austral Patagonia. 'The colonization of South America initially took place by entering with livestock through the western coast of the Pacific Ocean around 500 years ago,' said the study. 'Originally from the high Andean altitudes, cattle, donkeys, and mules were the animals most used for the transport of the mineral down to the Atlantic port of Buenos Aires for its further trans-ocean transport to Spain.' The study highlights that human endemic areas of fascioliasis have been described in Andean regions, mainly in high altitude areas of countries such as Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Ecuador, and Venezuela. However, human fascioliasis in Argentina is evidently in need for additional studies. 'A retrospective analysis highlights that its real epidemiological situation in high risk rural, mainly altitudinal areas, may currently be underestimated,' said the study. 'In fact, the description in the last years of some human hyperendemic areas revealed a far more complex situation than previously thought.'

title: Cancer : ce parasite silencieux qui infecte des millions de personnes dans le monde et qui inquiète les chercheurs
content: Schistosoma mansoni, the blood fluke, is a nearly invisible parasite that infects more than 250 million people worldwide, according to the World Health Organization (WHO) data for 2021. The parasite penetrates the skin without pain, remains undetected for long periods, and can cause severe organ damage and certain cancers, notably bladder cancer. Infection occurs when larvae from snails that have ingested human parasite eggs enter the skin during everyday activities such as swimming, washing, fishing or farming. The larvae mature and release thousands of eggs that trigger intense inflammatory reactions, leading to long‑term damage to the liver, bladder, kidneys and, in some cases, cancer. Symptoms—fever, cough, diarrhea, abdominal pain—are often mistaken for other tropical infections, contributing to under‑diagnosis and an estimated hundreds of thousands of deaths annually. A recent study from Tulane University revealed that the parasite inhibits the TRPV1+ protein, which normally transmits pain, heat and itch signals, allowing the parasite to evade both pain perception and the immune system. This discovery, published in *The Journal of Immunology*, may inspire new pain‑relief or anti‑inflammatory therapies. While historically confined to Africa and tropical regions, schistosomiasis is now emerging in Europe: recent cases have been reported in Spain, Portugal, southern France, and the United Kingdom, where 123 cases were recorded in 2022—almost triple the pre‑COVID‑19 level. Climate change is expanding the snail hosts’ habitats, raising public‑health concerns. The disease is treatable with praziquantel, which kills adult worms and reduces complications, but effectiveness depends on early diagnosis; delayed treatment increases the risk of irreversible sequelae.

title: Il parassita che penetra nella pelle senza dolore: la scoperta sul verme responsabile della schistosomiasi
content: A study by the Tulane School of Medicine has revealed how Schistosoma mansoni, a 17mm-long parasitic worm, is able to penetrate human skin without causing any pain or immune response. This parasite, also known as the 'blood fluke', causes intestinal schistosomiasis, a chronic disease that kills hundreds of thousands of people every year. According to the World Health Organization, in 2021, over 251 million people were infected, mainly in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean, and the Middle East. The infection occurs through contact with contaminated freshwater during daily activities such as swimming, washing clothes, or fishing. The larvae, developed in infected snails containing human feces, penetrate the skin and spread throughout the body, releasing thousands of eggs that can reach vital organs. A new study conducted on mice by researchers at the Tulane School of Medicine has explained why this worm does not cause pain or itching at the time of skin penetration. The results, published in The Journal of Immunology, show that the parasite reduces the activity of TRPV1+, a protein that normally sends signals to the brain of heat, pain, or itching. This ability allows the worm not only to be perceived by the host but also to evade the first defenses of the immune system, unlike other infectious agents that cause skin irritation or inflammation. According to Professor De'Broski R. Herbert, lead author of the study, studying these molecules could lead to the development of new non-opioid painkillers and medications to reduce the severity of schistosomiasis or other painful inflammatory diseases. Beyond African and South American endemic zones, the disease is spreading to the Middle East. In recent years, outbreaks have been reported in lakes and rivers in Spain, Portugal, and France, due to climate change that makes the water more favorable to the survival of infected snails. In the UK, cases are on the rise: in 2022, 123 cases were reported, more than double the previous year. According to Bonnie Webster, researcher at the Natural History Museum, the first European outbreaks would have been introduced by travelers from Africa, particularly from Senegal. Once a snail is infected, the entire local population can become a reservoir of the parasite, leading to the spread of the disease to entire human communities. The disease, also known as 'snail fever' or bilharziasis, can initially manifest with pruritic skin eruptions ('swimmer's itch'), fever, cough, diarrhea, muscle and abdominal pain. It is not the worms that directly cause the symptoms, but the body's reaction to the massive release of eggs. In severe cases, the infection can lead to infertility, blindness, organ damage, and even bladder cancer. Treatment consists of a drug called praziquantel, which eliminates adult worms. Prevention remains fundamental: avoiding bathing or immersing in potentially contaminated freshwater, while the risk is zero in the sea or chlorinated pools.

title: دودة قاتلة تختبئ في الماء وتخترق الجلد وتسبب السرطان..احذرها
content: A parasitic flatworm, known as the 'blood fluke', has been found to be able to penetrate human skin without causing any pain or itching, allowing it to enter the body and destroy it from the inside. The parasite, known as Schistosoma mansoni, is transmitted through contact with contaminated freshwater, such as during swimming, washing, or fishing. When infected individuals pass the parasite's eggs in their urine or feces, snails pick them up and transform into infectious larvae that can penetrate human skin upon contact. According to a recent scientific study, the parasite suppresses the activity of a nerve protein called TRPV1+, which is responsible for sending pain, heat, and itching signals to the brain. This suppression gives the parasite a double advantage: silent entry into the body and clever evasion of the immune system. Once inside the body, the parasite begins to release thousands of eggs, which can reach vital organs such as the liver, kidneys, bladder, and even the brain. The infection, known as schistosomiasis or bilharzia, can cause a range of symptoms from skin rashes and fever to organ damage, infertility, and anemia, and can develop into bladder cancer if left untreated. Despite the terror surrounding the parasite, scientists see its characteristics as a medical opportunity, with Dr. De Bruyne Herbert, the study's supervisor, stating that understanding how these parasites disable pain signals opens the door to developing effective painkillers, new anti-inflammatory agents, and even a preventive treatment against schistosomiasis. The threat is global and expanding, with the disease previously confined to Africa south of the Sahara now spreading to Europe and South America due to climate change and human travel. The UK has seen a significant increase in cases, with the number of cases doubling between 2021 and 2022. Prevention and awareness are essential, with the UK's National Health Service emphasizing the need to avoid swimming in untreated freshwater in infected areas, as the parasites cannot survive in saltwater or chlorinated pools. The effective treatment against these parasites is the drug 'praziquantel', and what appears to be calm water may hide an unseen danger. The parasites not only invade our bodies but also master the art of stealth and deception, making them one of the most fascinating and terrifying creatures...

title: Parasitic Infections Guide 2025
content: The 2025 Parasitic Infections Guide from healthhype.com outlines the global impact, symptoms, diagnosis, and prevention of parasitic infections affecting over 1.5 billion people annually. Ectoparasites like lice, mites, and ticks are highlighted for their role in causing itching, rashes, and disease transmission—such as Lyme disease and alpha-gal syndrome—with 2025 data showing a 15% rise in lice cases in schools. Effective treatments include permethrin shampoos for lice, ivermectin for scabies, and proper tick removal using tweezers. Helminths (parasitic worms), including roundworms, flukes, and tapeworms, are discussed in detail: roundworms cause abdominal pain and growth stunting, with albendazole curing 85–95% of cases; flukes like schistosomes lead to liver fibrosis and are diagnosed via stool or urine microscopy, treated with praziquantel; tapeworms, contracted from undercooked meat, can cause neurocysticercosis, managed with praziquantel or albendazole. Protozoal infections—malaria, leishmaniasis, and giardiasis—are emphasized as major threats, with malaria treated using artemisinin-based combinations and prevented via RTS,S vaccine and insecticide-treated bed nets. Giardiasis, spread through contaminated water, is managed with metronidazole or tinidazole. Zoonotic parasites such as Toxoplasma and Echinococcus, transmitted from animals, are addressed with serological testing and targeted treatments. The article stresses prevention through hygiene, safe food/water practices, vector control, and the One Health approach, citing a 20% drop in U.S. tick cases due to layered defenses. Overall, the guide promotes early detection, community action, and updated 2025 research to combat these hidden health threats.

title: بعد إعلان أول إصابة بـ"الدودة الحلزونية".. الأعراض وطرق الوقاية
content: On August 25, 2025, the U.S. Department of Health announced the first human case of the flesh‑fluke parasite, also known as the 'worm' parasite, in the United States. The parasite is caused by larvae of a parasitic fly that lay eggs on exposed wounds of warm‑blooded animals. The article reports that the female fly deposits 200–300 eggs in a single batch, with a lifetime total of up to 3,000 eggs. The larvae penetrate living flesh, feeding through their sharp mouths, and can kill the host if untreated. Symptoms include unexplained skin ulcers that do not heal, worsening wounds, pain, bleeding, a sensation of movement inside the wound, visible larvae, foul odor, and sometimes secondary bacterial infection with fever or chills. Prevention measures cited by Reuters and the CDC include avoiding insect bites in tropical or rural areas, keeping wounds clean and covered, wearing protective clothing, using EPA‑approved insect repellents, treating clothing and equipment with 0.5 % permethrin, and sleeping in screened or closed environments. Treatment requires prompt removal of larvae and thorough wound cleaning, with good chances of recovery if addressed early.

title: Prevalence and risk factors of sheep and goats fasciolosis in Ethiopia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
content: Fasciolosis, a parasitic disease caused by liver flukes, affects over 550 million ruminants globally, resulting in estimated annual economic losses of $3.2 billion. In Ethiopia, where sheep and goats are crucial for food security and income, fasciolosis causes chronic illness, reducing productivity and fertility. The disease also has zoonotic potential, with humans becoming infected through contaminated water or vegetables. The life cycle of Fasciola species involves freshwater snails, and climate factors play a central role in shaping transmission risk. In Ethiopia, fasciolosis is endemic, with F. hepatica predominating in highland areas and F. gigantica in lowland regions. Traditional pastoral practices and limited veterinary services contribute to sustained transmission. This study aims to generate a comprehensive national estimate of fasciolosis prevalence among sheep and goats in Ethiopia and identify epidemiological factors influencing its distribution. The findings will facilitate evidence-based improvements in diagnostic approaches, therapeutic strategies, and targeted interventions, aligning with global efforts to mitigate the impact of zoonotic diseases. As stated by the authors, 'This study provides essential insights for veterinary professionals, policymakers, and researchers, facilitating evidence-based improvements in diagnostic approaches, therapeutic strategies, and prioritization of targeted, region-specific interventions.'

title: Wenn erst einmal der Wurm drin ist
content: Studies show that 80% of examined biological animal husbandry systems and nearly 90% of chicken breeding operations are infested with Ascarids. A single female worm in a pig's intestine can produce hundreds of thousands of eggs per day, which survive in the soil for 10 to 12 years, remaining infectious. Historically, cage systems for chickens and non-artificially structured pig housing limited contact with feces, offering some protection against infection—a situation now seen as tragically outdated. Ascaris suum, found in pigs, is a zoonotic parasite capable of infecting humans, posing risks to children playing on farms or farmers themselves. Spreading 'good organic manure' for garden fertilization or eating unwashed root vegetables like carrots from organic farms is therefore discouraged. In contrast, Ascaridia galli, the chicken worm, does not infect humans. The interconnected health of humans, animals, and the environment is exemplified by soil-transmitted helminth infections, which are the focus of a newly funded German Research Foundation Graduated Research College titled 'One-Health Approach for Soil-Transmitted Helminths.' This initiative strengthens the 'Global Health' research focus within the Berlin University Alliance's Excellence Cluster. The program will train veterinarians, biologists, health system researchers, and economists in Germany and at three Medical Research Institutes in Kenya. At the Free University, research will examine infections in pigs and chickens from birth to slaughter, environmental impacts, and effects on wildlife. In collaboration with Kenyan institutes, the study will also analyze health impacts of Ascarid infections in children from birth to age five. Researchers will compare animal and human infections, study immune responses, metabolic changes in worms, and host-microbiome interactions. The team aims to determine whether the same beneficial bacteria support worms across species—humans, pigs, and chickens. Mathematical modeling will assess climate change impacts on infection spread and how organic farms affect local wildlife. Previous studies in Hungary found 50% of animals in nature parks were infected; the project will investigate whether wild boars in the Berlin area are similarly affected. Soil sample analyses will complement theoretical models.

title: Liver flukes: A mountain of unseen problems
content: Liver flukes (Fasciola hepatica) pose a significant threat to cattle health and productivity, causing liver damage, reduced nutrient conversion, lower conception rates, weight loss, and increased susceptibility to diseases such as redwater, which results from Clostridium novyii type D toxin destroying red blood cells and causing reddish urine. According to Dr. DL Step, DVM of Boehringer Ingelheim, liver flukes can suppress the immune system, making cattle more vulnerable to respiratory diseases and other pathogens. The fluke life cycle, lasting five or more months, involves eggs in manure, development in Lymnaeid snails (Pseudosuccinea columella), and transmission via grass or water to cattle, where juvenile flukes migrate to the liver and mature in bile ducts. Clinical signs include poor body condition despite adequate nutrition, reduced milk production in cow-calf operations, lower weaning weights, decreased average daily gain in feedlots, and higher days on feed. Liver condemnations at slaughter are also common. Diagnosis requires a specialized 'fluke finder' fecal test, as routine flotation tests are ineffective. Treatment is most effective when timed to regional climate patterns: mid-September to early November in the Southeast and early spring (around March) in the Northwest. IVOMEC® PLUS (ivermectin and clorsulon) is highlighted as a dewormer effective against adult liver flukes and over 30 species of internal and external parasites. Dr. Step emphasizes the importance of a two-pronged treatment approach and working with a veterinarian to develop a region-specific control protocol. Safety warnings include not treating cattle within 21 days of slaughter, and avoiding use in female dairy cattle of breeding age and veal calves.
